[[File:Andrew Crumey.jpg|thumb|Andrew Crumey in 2021]] 
'''Andrew Crumey''' (born 1961) is a Scottish [[novelist]] and former [[literary editor]] of the [[Edinburgh]] newspaper ''[[Scotland on Sunday]]''.
His works of [[literary fiction]] incorporate elements of [[speculative fiction]], [[historical fiction]], [[philosophical fiction]] and [[Menippean satire]]. [[Brian Stableford]] has called them "philosophical fantasies".<ref>Brian Stableford, The A to Z of Fantasy Literature. Scarecrow Press (2009). p191</ref>  The Spanish newspaper [[El Mundo (Spain)|El Mundo]] called Crumey "one of the most interesting and original European authors of recent years."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://signin.lexisnexis.com/lnaccess/app/signin?back=https%3A%2F%2Fadvance.lexis.com%3A443%2Fdocument%2F%3Fpdmfid%3D1519360%26crid%3D5b87645c-61ba-441e-82df-5463f15d9ccc%26pddocfullpath%3D%2Fshared%2Fdocument%2Fnews%2Furn%3AcontentItem%3A49F7-0N20-01H9-G05F-00000-00%26pdcontentcomponentid%3D256121%26pdteaserkey%3Dsr0%26pditab%3Dallpods%26ecomp%3Dzxmyk%26earg%3Dsr0%26prid%3D479c8839-8cac-4b85-96da-41c183b748de&aci=la|title=Lexis® - Sign In &#124; LexisNexis|website=signin.lexisnexis.com}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Crumey was born in [[Glasgow]], Scotland, and grew up in [[Kirkintilloch]]. He graduated with First Class Honours from the [[University of St Andrews]] and holds a [[PhD]] in [[theoretical physics]] from [[Imperial College]], [[London]]. His thesis was on [[integrable systems]] and [[Kac-Moody algebras]], supervised by [[David Olive]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://crumey.co.uk/archive/articles/Crumey-ADWB-1988-PhD-Thesis.pdf|title=Integrable Dynamical Systems Associated With Kac-Moody Algebras|website=crumey.co.uk}}</ref>

Crumey's first novel, ''[[Music, in a Foreign Language]]'', won the Saltire Society First Book Award in 1994.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.dedalusbooks.com/our-books/video.php?id=00000025&id2=00000005|title=Music, in a Foreign Language by Andrew Crumey : Our Books :: Dedalus Books, Publishers of Literary Fiction|website=www.dedalusbooks.com}}</ref> Its theme of [[alternate history]] was inspired by the [[many-worlds]] interpretation of quantum mechanics.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://www.northumbria.ac.uk/about-us/our-staff/c/andrew-crumey/|title=Andrew Crumey|website=www.northumbria.ac.uk}}</ref>

His second novel ''[[Pfitz]]'' was a New York Times "Notable Book of the Year" in 1997, described as "cerebral but warm and likeable".<ref>{{cite web | title=Notable Books of the Year 1997 | website=The New York Times Web Archive | date=2018-04-08 | url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/97/12/07/reviews/notable-fiction.html?_r=1 | access-date=2025-08-27}}</ref> The sequel, ''[[D'Alembert's Principle (novel)|D'Alembert's Principle]]'' took its title from a principle of physics.

Crumey was a regular book reviewer for Scotland on Sunday from 1996 and became the newspaper's literary editor in 2000. He won an Arts Council of England Writers' Award, worth £7,000.<ref>The Times (London). Friday, May 12, 2000.</ref>

In 2000 Crumey's fourth novel ''[[Mr Mee]]'' was longlisted for the Man Booker Prize and won the Scottish Arts Council Book Award.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://researchportal.northumbria.ac.uk/en/prizes/scottish-arts-council-book-award|title=Scottish Arts Council Book Award|website=Northumbria University Research Portal}}</ref> He followed it with ''[[Mobius Dick]]'', described by [[Joseph O'Connor]] as "perhaps the only novel about quantum mechanics you could imagine reading while lying on a beach."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dedalusbooks.com/our-books/reviews.php?id=00000256|title=Mobius Dick by Andrew Crumey : Our Books :: Dedalus Books, Publishers of Literary Fiction|website=www.dedalusbooks.com}}</ref>

In 2003 Crumey was selected for Granta's "Best of Young British Novelists", but had been incorrectly submitted by publisher Picador, being over 40 at the time.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2013/apr/06/then-now-granta-best-novelists|title=Then and now: Granta's best young British novelists|date=6 April 2013|newspaper=The Guardian}}</ref>

In 2006, Crumey became the fifth recipient of the [[Northern Rock Foundation]] Writer's Award for [[Sputnik Caledonia]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://literaryreview.co.uk/dreams-of-space|title=Matt Thorne - Dreams of Space|website=Literary Review}}</ref> which was also shortlisted for the James Tait Black Memorial Prize<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ed.ac.uk/news/all-news/james-tait-black-140509|title=Nobel winner in running for book prize|website=The University of Edinburgh}}</ref> and Scottish Book of the Year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.heraldscotland.com/default_content/12384989.new-sponsor-announced-pound-30-000-book-awards/|title=New sponsor announced for £30,000 book awards|website=HeraldScotland|date=6 March 2009 }}</ref>

In 2006 he became lecturer in [[creative writing]] at [[Newcastle University]]. In 2011 he was a visiting fellow at [[Institute of Advanced Study (Durham)|Durham Institute of Advanced Study]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iasdurham.org/people/former-fellows/futures-i-fellows/dr-andrew-crumey/|title=Dr Andrew Crumey &#124; IAS Durham}}</ref> then became lecturer in creative writing at [[Northumbria University]].<ref name="auto"/> It was during this time that he wrote ''[[The Secret Knowledge]]'', published in 2013.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

His PhD students at Newcastle and Northumbria Universities have included Alex Lockwood,<ref>
{{Cite web|url=https://www.collectiveinkbooks.com/roundfire-books/authors/alex-lockwood|title=Alex Lockwood, Roundfire Books| access-date = 17 September 2023}}</ref> [[Guy Mankowski]]<ref name="auto1">{{cite web |url=https://www.northumbria.ac.uk/about-us/our-staff/c/andrew-crumey/ |title=Andrew Crumey |website=Northumbria University |access-date=17 September 2023}}</ref> and John Schoneboom<ref name="auto1"/>

He has an interest in astronomy and in 2014 he published on the subject of astronomic visibility and [[Ricco's law]].<ref>Crumey, A. (2014). {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20141224152522/http://mnras.oxfordjournals.org/content/442/3/2600.full.pdf+html|title=Human contrast threshold and astronomical visibility.}} MNRAS 442, 2600–2619.</ref>

His short story Singularity was broadcast on Radio 4 in 2016<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b07dp1rr|title=BBC Radio 4 - Singularity by Andrew Crumey|website=BBC}}</ref> and later published in ''[[The Great Chain of Unbeing]]''.

In 2017 he was a contestant in the St Andrews team on BBC Two's Christmas University Challenge.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b09l933l|title=BBC Two - University Challenge, Christmas 2017, Selwyn College, Cambridge v St Andrews University|website=BBC}}</ref>

In 2018 ''[[The Great Chain of Unbeing]]'' was shortlisted for the Saltire Fiction Award.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.saltiresociety.org.uk/scotlands-national-book-awards-2018-fiction-shortlist|title=Scotland's National Book Awards 2018: Fiction Shortlist|website=The Saltire Society|date=6 January 2021 }}</ref> [[Adam Roberts (British writer)|Adam Roberts]] wrote in [[Literary Review]]: 'Andrew Crumey's new book is a quasi-novel built out of connected short stories. It's something for which we English have no specific term, but for which German critics have probably coined an impressively resonant piece of nomenclature (''Kurzgeschichtenverkettung'', maybe?). It's as good an example of the form as I know.'

In 2023 he published his ninth novel, ''[[Beethoven's Assassins]]'', described in ''[[The Irish Times]]'' as "a deliciously intellectual, ambitious book that explores time, metaphysics, narrative and pretty much everything, all at once."<ref>{{cite news |last=McKee |first=Ruth |date= 19 August 2023 |title=Beethoven's Assassins by Andrew Crumey: A deliciously intellectual and ambitious book |url=https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/books/review/2023/08/19/beethovens-assassins-by-andrew-crumey-a-deliciously-intellectual-and-ambitious-book/ |newspaper=The Irish Times |location=Dublin |access-date=17 September 2023}}</ref>

In 2025 he completed the late [[Robert_Irwin_(writer)|Robert Irwin's]] unfinished novel ''Rapture of the Deep''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dedalusbooks.com/our-books/book.php?id=00000406|title=Rapture of the Deep|website=Dedalus Books}}</ref> Michael Caines wrote in the [[Times Literary Supplement]], "Andrew Crumey testifies that ''Rapture of the Deep'', his completion of this unfinished work, is half Irwin and half Crumey, at least in its word count."<ref>{{cite news |last=Caines |first=Michael |date= 20 March 2026 |title=All of the vision: A collaboration of ideas and incidents |url=https://www.the-tls.com/regular-features/in-brief/rapture-of-the-deep-robert-irwin-andrew-crumey-book-review-michael-caines |newspaper=Times Literary Supplement |location=London |access-date=8 June 2026}}</ref>

==Critical reception==

[[Jonathan Coe]] described Crumey as "a writer more interested in inheriting the mantle of [[Georges Perec|Perec]] and [[Milan Kundera|Kundera]] than [[Martin Amis|Amis]] and [[Margaret Drabble|Drabble]]... Crumey seems so untouched by the post-war British tradition that he simply writes as if it never existed."<ref>Jonathan Coe, The Guardian. August 16, 1994</ref>

''The Cambridge Companion to British Fiction Since 1945'', commenting on unorthodox approaches to genre fiction by writers including Crumey, [[Frank Kuppner]] and [[Ken Macleod]], said "Andrew Crumey is one of the most innovative and engaging Scottish writers to emerge out of this context in the last twenty years. His speculative fiction has a strong European and global dimension, drawing on the influence of [[Borges]], [[Calvino]] and [[Milorad Pavić]] in its intricate, nested narratives, non-linearity, and ludic encyclopaedism."<ref>{{cite book | last=James | first=David | title=The Cambridge Companion to British Fiction since 1945 | publisher=Cambridge University Press | date=2015-10-08 | isbn=978-1-107-56271-4 | page=}}</ref>

In ''Twenty-First-century Fiction: Contemporary British Voices'', Daniel Lea put Crumey in a list of "post-postmodernist" British writers that included [[Iain Banks]], [[Bernardine Evaristo]] and [[Neil Gaiman]], characterised by an "intermingling of genre and literary fiction."<ref>{{cite book | last=Lea | first=Daniel | title=Twenty-first-century Fiction: Contemporary British Voices | publisher=Manchester University Press | date=2017 | isbn=978-0-7190-8149-1 | page=}}</ref>

Bent Sorensen bracketed Crumey with another physicist-turned-novelist, [[Alan Lightman]], and discussed their move from science to literature using [[Pierre Bourdieu]]'s concepts of "field", "position-taking" and "gatekeeping". Sorensen wrote that Crumey was "opposed to the postmodern epistemology when asked to define his world-view in philosophical terms... his fictional practice, however, can still fairly be characterized as postmodern."<ref>{{cite journal | last=Sørensen | first=Bent | title=Physicists in the Field of Fiction | journal=Comparative Critical Studies | volume=2 | issue=2 | date=2005 | issn=1744-1854 | doi=10.3366/ccs.2005.2.2.241 | pages=241–255 | url=https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/ccs.2005.2.2.241 | access-date=2025-08-27| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Timothy C. Baker described Crumey's novels as "monadological", citing [[Deleuze]]'s reading of [[Leibniz]], and observing that "The relation between [Crumey's] novels is unusual: five of his seven novels explore, in various ways, the legacies of Enlightenment thought, often drawing upon the same ideas and figures. These novels, crucially, do not amount to a sequence, nor is the relation between events in them ever straightforwardly causal. Instead, each novel covers similar ground in a series of overlapping folds, while remaining narratively distinct."<ref>Baker, Timothy C. "Harmonic Monads: Reading Contemporary Scottish Fiction through the Enlightenment." Scottish Literary Review, vol. 9 no. 1, 2017, p. 95-113. Project MUSE, https://muse.jhu.edu/article/659099.</ref>

Cultural theorist Sonia Front wrote, "The notion of parallel universes seems to be Andrew Crumey's favourite physical theory... His writings can be seen as a [[multiverse]] themselves, with the characters reappearing to live an alternative world-line in another novel."<ref>{{cite book | last=Front | first=Sonia | title=Shapes of Time in British Twenty-First Century Quantum Fiction | publisher=Cambridge Scholars Publishing | date=2015-09-04 | isbn=978-1-4438-8203-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books/about/Shapes_of_Time_in_British_Twenty_First_C.html?id=1IHWCgAAQBAJ | access-date=2025-08-27 | pages=37–72}}</ref>

Florian Kläger sees "a self-reflexive cosmopoetics of the novel" in the writings of Crumey, [[Martin Amis]], [[John Banville]], [[Zadie Smith]] and [[Jeanette Winterson]].<ref>{{cite book | last=Klaeger | first=Florian | title=Reading Into the Stars | publisher=Universitatsverlag Winter | date=2018 | isbn=978-3-8253-6890-6 | url=https://www.winter-verlag.de/en/detail/978-3-8253-6890-6/Klaeger_Reading_into_the_Stars/ | page=}}</ref>

<!-- Suggest we move the following to the articles on the novels they discuss...

Mark C. Taylor related the multiple "authors" in ''Pfitz'' to complexity theory. "''Pfitz'' is not just ''about'' emergent complexity but is a brilliant enactment of it. One of the strategies Crumey and his coauthors use to generate complexity is to create multiple self-reflexive loops by folding authors and readers into each other until the line separating them becomes obscure."<ref>Mark C. Taylor. The Moment of Complexity. University of Chicago Press, 2003.</ref>

Stephen J. Burn sees Crumey's [[Pfitz]], [[Tom_McCarthy_(novelist)|Tom McCarthy's]] ''Men in Space'' and [[David_Mitchell_(author)|David Mitchell's]] ''Number9Dream'' as examples of a subgenre he terms "multiple drafts" novels, with [[Pfitz]] being "the earliest—and arguably the most representative—example of this form." Burn's term "multiple drafts" is borrowed from [[Daniel Dennett]]'s model of consciousness. Burn writes that [[Pfitz]] shows "evident familiarity with Daniel Dennett's work" and says it "might be considered to provide the hidden internal blueprint for different levels of the novel's action."<ref>Stephen J. Burn. Reading the Multiple Drafts Novel. MFS Modern Fiction Studies. Johns Hopkins University Press. Volume 58, Number 3, Fall 2012 pp. 436-458</ref>

Toon Staes sees ''Pfitz'' as a "systems novel", a term coined by [[Tom LeClair]] who applied it to writers including [[Don DeLillo]], [[Thomas Pynchon]], [[John Barth]] and [[Ursula Le Guin]]. In Staes' usage, "systems novels feature multiple nonlinear and fragmented narrative strands that gradually fix the reader's attention on a network of relationships," with ''Pfitz'' being "an interesting test case."<ref>Toon Staes. Narrative Complexity and the Case of Pfitz: An Update for the 'Systems Novel'. Interlitteraria 2021, 26/1: 295-308</ref>

Timothy C. Baker comments on the use of [[Gothic fiction|Gothic]] tropes such as found manuscripts in the work of Crumey and other Scottish writers. "Use of such tropes can be limiting... In other texts, however, including [[Alasdair Gray| Gray's]] ''Poor Things'', Crumey's ''Mr Mee'', and [[A. L. Kennedy]]'s ''So I Am Glad'', each of which embeds Gothic elements in another genre or mode, the trope exceeds these limitations and allows for a greater reflection on the relationship between language and experience."<ref>Timothy C. Baker. Contemporary Scottish Gothic: Mourning, Authenticity, and Tradition. Palgrave Macmillan (2014).</ref> Baker sees Crumey's novels as "monadological", citing [[Deleuze]]'s reading of [[Leibniz]], and observing that "The relation between [Crumey's] novels is unusual: five of his seven novels explore, in various ways, the legacies of Enlightenment thought, often drawing upon the same ideas and figures. These novels, crucially, do not amount to a sequence, nor is the relation between events in them ever straightforwardly causal. Instead, each novel covers similar ground in a series of overlapping folds, while remaining narratively distinct."<ref>Timothy C. Baker. Harmonic Monads: Reading Contemporary Scottish
Fiction through the Enlightenment. Scottish Literary Review, vol. 9, no. 1, pp. 95-113. (2017)</ref>

Lisa Harrison compares Crumey's ''Sputnik Caledonia'' with [[ Matthew Fit]]t's ''But'n'Ben A-Go-Go''. "Their fictive worlds are Scotland, though not as we know it - they each present a Scotland stripped of stereotyping, thus reformed and redefined through fiction."<ref>Lisa Harrison in ''Scotland as Science Fiction'' edited by Caroline McCracken-Flesher. Bucknell University Press, 2012.</ref>

Commenting on the story "The Last Midgie on Earth" in ''The Great Chain of Unbeing'', Milena Kalicanin writes, "Scotland becomes Crumey's synonym for a [[postmodern]] [[utopia]] that he symbolically defines as a state of mind, a land of spiritual freedom in which everybody says an everlasting 'yes' to life, and a profound 'no' to the postmodern [[capitalist]] system of values."<ref>Milena Kalicanin. Uncovering Caledonia: An Introduction to Scottish Studies. Cambridge Scholars Publishing (2019)</ref>
